explanation: Fires on a short letter/alphabetic suffix token that directly follows a run of digits: unit and ordinal suffixes (150[[cc]], 80[[g]], 44[[k]], 21[[st]], timestamp [[Z]]) and letters inside hex IDs or part numbers (HMC5883[[L]], 1234[[a]]). Strongest when the letter attaches to the digits with no space. A letter after a mixed alphanumeric string gives a moderate response. Ordinary words and punctuation give near zero.

Fires on separators (a space, comma or minus) between numbers in dense numeric lists, coordinate strings and tables. By far the strongest case is a space between numbers in an SVG path ('0.55[[ ]]0.45'). Other number-separator positions give only a moderate response (15-30%). Weak, scattered responses also appear on code tokens and filler words.

Fires on a word in the middle of a technical or scientific sentence, typically the noun or determiner just after a preposition or verb ('using[[ key]] words', 'low[[ density]] environment', 'exposure to[[ serotonin]]', 'poor[[ channel]] environment'). It also fires on code and comment tokens such as 'Copyright (C[[)]]'. I see no clear lexical rule; it seems to track a broad expository technical-prose context rather than a specific token.

Fires on the second or later token of a multi-token unit whose completion is highly predictable from what came before. Examples: the rest of a name or phrase (John[[ McCain]], West[[ Indies]], Sierra[[ Leone]], heter[[ogeneity]]), code identifiers and paths (testify[[/assert]], http[[-equiv]], [[.getBoundingClientRect]]), and German articles after prepositions (nach[[ dem]], auf[[ dem]]). A token that starts something new or is unpredictable gives a weak response.

Fires on mid-word subword pieces of rare proper names or technical words (Gr[[imal]]dis, k[[un]]zisoft, Sch[[um]]acher, ne[[opt]]erin, gemcit[[ab]]ine). It also fires on digits inside numbers, dates and timestamps, typically the second token of a number ('base [[1]]1', '([[1]]958'). It responds when the token continues a fragment begun by the previous token, and barely at all on ordinary whole words.

Fires on a heterogeneous set of content tokens: word-completion pieces in medical/scientific terms (Lymph[[ob]]lastic, hypere[[cho]]ic, backsc[[attered]]), the word COPYRIGHT in BSD license boilerplate, and nouns completing noun phrases in technical text (rounded[[ corners]], AWS[[ account]], warranty[[ return]]). I see no single shared feature.

Fires on the term or operand right after an operator in polynomial and algebra expressions (the coefficient after '-' or '+' in 's**3 -[[ ]]8*s**2'). It also fires on a function word or preposition that links two noun phrases in prose ('a friend[[ of]] mine', 'institute[[ of]]', 'Gy[[ per]] fraction', 'from[[ this]] software'). The two jobs share only a loose 'connective in a relation' theme.

Fires most strongly on exponents and linear terms in auto-generated polynomial definitions of the form 'Let f(x) = ... x**[[2]] + ...[[*x]]', especially the exponent after '**' and the '*var' term. It responds more weakly (around 50%) to scattered tokens in prose and code (innate, 'Development[[ Status]]', worst-case[[ space]]).

Fires on a token that completes a highly conventional fixed construction. Main cases: 'most' in superlatives ('their[[ most]] recent', 'world's[[ most]]'); the package or import name after 'package'/'import'/'using namespace' ([[ com]], [[ React]], [[ std]], [[ pandas]]); the hyphen in Bootstrap 'col-md[[-]]8' classes; 'In doing[[ so]]'. These look like several unrelated habits.

Fires on miscellaneous tokens in boilerplate and code: license text ('the Corporation[[ nor]]', 'names[[ of]] its contributors', 'may be[[ reproduced]]'), identifiers and parameters in code (offset, class, Try, '= initialState'), and some prose tokens. I find no consistent rule beyond 'mid-phrase token in formulaic or technical text'.

Fires on the indentation whitespace token that starts a new key line inside a jQuery $.ajax({...}) options object or similar config blocks (before url:, success:, cache:). It also fires on tokens in HTTP header and request setup ('Content[[-type]]', 'MIME', 'new BasicCredentialsProvider', OAuth URLs). The context is building an HTTP request in code. A weak response appears on mid-name pieces of proper names.

Fires on list-closing or open-ended continuation words: 'among other', 'and so on', 'or[[ its]] affiliates', 'Plus', 'something like[[ it]]'. It also fires on tokens inside formatted strings and tables: digits in version numbers and SHA-256, ':' in timestamps, and '+' at the start of ASCII table border lines. Two unrelated jobs.

Fires on the token that completes a well-known multi-token name or term: institution and proper names (Georgia Bureau[[ of]] Investigation, United States[[ Navy]], Harry[[ Potter]]), medical and chemical word pieces (bul[[los]]a, hyperparathy[[roid]]ism), and fixed technical strings (boost/property[[_tree]], '-' list items in YAML bibliographies). It responds when the token is strongly determined by a named-entity context.

Fires on scattered tokens: the first digit after a minus sign in arithmetic answers, byte-fragment tokens of CJK characters, '(' before unit conversions ('kms[[ (]]110 miles'), mid-word pieces of names, and assorted function words. I see no common thread.
